Access, Capacity, Learning

Complete discussion notebook ·

Help useful work reach its next step.

Three priorities for the next five years: widen access, build capacity, and make learning easier to use.

These are proposals drawn from my work in independent research, open-source software, and community partnerships. Choose a priority above, then a topic to bring into the discussion.

A point to bring to the room

Support should connect people to a useful next step—and leave enough evidence to show what that support changed.

From discussion to a practical pilot

The convening asks us to name barriers, understand their causes, identify an intervention and its partners, and define progress. The three priorities above follow that structure.

Access focuses on supported referrals. Capacity focuses on engineering and validation. Learning focuses on reusable evidence and better decisions about continued support.

These are participant proposals for the National Innovation Roadmap. Track tags indicate where a topic may fit; they are editorial suggestions.

Independent researchers

Who has useful work but cannot reach the people, infrastructure, or support needed to advance it?

My example

Good work starts in places without a grants office: a home lab, an open-source project, a small nonprofit. Being eligible for a program is not the same as having a usable path into it.

Question for the room. Who owns the first handoff when someone has promising work but no institution behind them?

A practical next step

Pilot a supported referral path for independent researchers and small teams. Record where the handoff breaks down.

Progress would mean: Time to a useful connection; completed handoffs; reasons people are turned away.

Who needs to be involved

Program navigators, independent researchers, research institutions, and regional partners.

Research stage: Discovery → Translation.

More context

  • Useful work can start outside universities, established companies, and federal laboratories.
  • Independent contributors usually lack grants staff, technology-transfer offices, institutional infrastructure, and professional introductions.
  • Evaluate applicants on relevant evidence, capability, and potential contribution, not affiliation alone.

Evidence and technical detail

Breakout point 2 asks for root causes. A barrier to investigate is the assumption that an institution supplies staff, infrastructure, and introductions. Its importance will vary by program and applicant.

Breakout pointContribution
1. ChallengeCapable independent contributors cannot convert eligibility into entry.
2. Root causeSupport systems assume institutional affiliation and staff.
3. Existing modelsSBIR/STTR for small businesses; OSF and Registered Reports for open research practice.
4. GapIdentify where individuals, informal teams, and small nonprofits lack an accountable handoff.
5. RecommendationSupported entry pathways with a named navigator.
6. StakeholdersNSF TIP, SBIR/STTR, EPSCoR institutions, open-source foundations, community organizations.
7. MeasuresCompleted connections and progress toward validation, not portal visits.

Finding support

How can we reduce the time spent finding the right program or partner?

My example

One front door for funding, compute, storage, technical help, research partners, and commercialization support. The important part is not the website. It is the named person or office responsible for what happens after the match.

proposed

A practical next step

Connect existing directories to a named navigator who can make a warm referral and confirm the outcome.

Progress would mean: Referrals that reach a suitable partner, rather than portal visits alone.

Who needs to be involved

Program staff, technical assistance providers, and people seeking support.

Research stage: Across the research journey.

More context

  • Profiles for individuals, informal open-source teams, nonprofits, and small businesses.
  • Opportunity records that state eligibility, affiliation rules, resources offered, and when those details were last verified.
  • Matching by the contributor's actual need: compute, storage, validation, research partner, maintenance funding, or commercialization support.
  • A named navigator or receiving organization responsible for following through.
  • Tracking whether a referral produced a useful connection, and why unsuccessful referrals stopped.

Evidence and technical detail

Funding search already exists, for example Simpler.Grants.gov. The proposal adds what search cannot do: responsibility for the handoff. AI can help discover and explain matches. Program owners stay responsible for eligibility decisions and ambiguous cases.

Portal functionWho does itWhy
Find and explain candidate matchesAI assistanceFast, broad, cheap to repeat
Eligibility determinationProgram ownerAccountable, appealable
Ambiguous or consequential casesHuman navigatorJudgment and follow-through
Referral outcome trackingPortal recordShows where applicants get stuck

A concrete use case appears later on this site: a nonprofit with a community and worthwhile questions, but no research partner.

Open-source stewardship

What support keeps a research tool usable after its first release?

My example

Research runs on software that someone has to test, document, secure, maintain, and support. That work is what lets a discovery be used by other researchers, nonprofits, businesses, and public agencies.

A practical next step

Treat maintenance, documentation, testing, and user support as explicit work in a bounded pilot.

Progress would mean: External reuse, maintenance continuity, and reproducible results.

Who needs to be involved

Maintainers, research software engineers, users, and funding partners.

Research stage: Translation → Adoption.

More context

  • Maintenance and adoption work deserve recognition alongside new inventions.
  • Support should reach the people maintaining critical dependencies, including independent contributors.
  • Reuse lowers adoption costs for everyone downstream.

Evidence and technical detail

Open-source projects provide reusable research tools. Maintaining them can require testing, documentation, security work, and support that a research grant does not always cover. The proposal is to recognize and fund that work explicitly.

The Mojo ports and Rust/Mojo development attempts in this portfolio offer cases for discussion. They do not establish that every rewrite improves performance or that every open-source project lacks funding.

Software qualification

What evidence is needed before a promising tool is ready for the next stage?

My example

We rewrote part of our scientific computing tools in Mojo and checked the new version against the established one. Across 24 test cases the two programs gave exactly the same answers. That was only the first test.

We then compared the answers with independent mathematical references. The higher-precision version passed. The lower-precision version failed.

Two programs can agree perfectly and still miss the target. Agreement and accuracy are different questions.

documented

Scope: S02-I, 20 August 2026. Overall protocol: failed. Applies to the tested stencil and environment. No new GPU run, speed qualification, or physical-feasibility finding.

Sources: Pinned qualification report

A practical next step

Use a small qualification case with fixed criteria. Keep agreement, numerical accuracy, and performance as separate claims.

Progress would mean: A reviewer can identify the tested scope, failed criteria, and evidence needed for the next decision.

Who needs to be involved

Domain researchers, numerical specialists, software engineers, and prospective users.

Research stage: Translation → Validation.

More context

Think of two calculators showing the same answer. That is encouraging: they are consistent. But if both round away a small number that matters, both give the same wrong answer. Agreement is a useful check. Accuracy needs an independent reference.

CheckResultPlain meaning
Same input bytes read by both programsPass, 24 of 24Both started from the same data
Same output bytesPass, 24 of 24No disagreement between HIP and Mojo
Float64 against independent referencePassHigher precision met the pre-set limits
Float32 against independent referenceFailLower precision exceeded the limits
Overall protocolFailThe full requirement set was not met
SpeedNot qualified hereNo performance qualification is established by these results
  • Modernization should fix a shown limitation in correctness, maintainability, portability, security, or performance. Language choice alone proves nothing.
  • The accuracy limits were set before the run, so any later change to those limits requires a new protocol version.
  • The failed result is kept and published. It records which tested criteria passed and which need further work.

Evidence and technical detail

The tested operation is a stencil: it compares a grid point with its neighbors to estimate how a quantity changes across space. Such calculations subtract nearly equal numbers and then magnify what remains, so rounding matters even in a single evaluation. Float32 keeps about seven significant digits; Float64 keeps about 15 to 16.

Campaign S02-I covered two precisions, three grid sizes (64³, 128³, 256³), and four input families (quadratic, normalized cubic, asymmetric, sinusoidal), with analytic and independent CPU references.

PrecisionMax relative L2 errorFrozen limitMax scaled L∞ errorFrozen limit
Float645.98 × 10⁻¹²1 × 10⁻¹¹5.83 × 10⁻¹¹1 × 10⁻¹⁰
Float322.32488 × 10⁻³1 × 10⁻⁴1.5625 × 10⁻²1 × 10⁻³

Float32 exceeded its limits by roughly 23 and 16 times. The repository attributes the shared failure to finite-precision conditioning and proposes a dedicated study of cancellation, scaling, and resolution.

Options on the table

OptionBenefitRequired check
Use Float64 now for the qualified stencilAlready meets the accuracy gatesTwice the memory per value; real speed cost depends on hardware
Reformulate the calculationMay preserve small differences without extra precision everywhereAlgebraically equal expressions can behave differently on a computer
Mixed precisionCould cut memory and compute costCannot restore detail already lost in Float32 inputs
Stronger independent referencesLocates the error sourceThe reference itself needs validation
Benchmark after accuracy passesEvidence-based cost decisionsHardware changes do not fix low-precision arithmetic

Three separate questions stay separate: do HIP and Mojo agree; do their answers meet an independent reference; does the model agree with physical evidence? This campaign answers the first two for one kernel on one system. It says nothing about physical feasibility.

Evidence and decisions

How can a partnership show why it made a decision, and revise it when evidence changes?

My example

When AI helps with research, someone later has to ask: what evidence supports this claim, what is still uncertain, and what was this action allowed to do? GKOS is my developing approach to keeping those links.

Provenance lets people inspect a claim. It does not make the claim true.

in development

A practical next step

Test one evidence record that connects a claim, its sources, review, limits, and next decision.

Progress would mean: A new reviewer can trace the claim to evidence and explain what changed after review.

Who needs to be involved

Researchers, evidence reviewers, tool builders, and the people using the result.

Research stage: Across the research journey.

More context

  • AI-assisted work needs records of sources, transformations, checks, authorization, and resulting actions.
  • Reviewers should be able to see what supports a claim, what remains uncertain, and what an action was authorized to do.
  • Corrections stay visible as new versions instead of silently rewriting history.

Evidence and technical detail

RepositoryRoleStatus
gkos-standardPre-standard for evidence lineage, authority, dispositions, governance responsibilities, conformance fixturesdocumented
GKOS-EngineTypeScript reference engine: parsing, validation, lineage, knowledge graph, retrieval, citationsdocumented
GKOS-Engine-RustGround-up Rust implementation; implementation and qualification records; consult the current repository for statusin development
GKOS-Engine-LiteRust retrieval and restricted-profile work; conformance and adversarial casesin development
model-capability-manifest-standardDeclare AI capability through structured, testable, versioned evidence rather than model namesproposed

Proposed division of labor: AI extracts metadata and proposes classifications and related records; deterministic checks enforce allowed values, required evidence, and consistency; humans review ambiguity and consequential interpretation. Deterministic rules can enforce record integrity. They cannot make scientific interpretation automatically correct, so conflicting interpretations stay attributable and inspectable.

AI and verification

Where can AI reduce friction, and where must human judgment remain?

My example

AI can accelerate code, analysis, documentation, and proposed experiments. Checking that output still takes time and expertise. Confidence and a fluent explanation are not acceptance criteria.

Question for the room. As producing research artifacts becomes cheaper, how do we keep checking them from becoming the next bottleneck?

A practical next step

Pair AI-assisted work with deterministic checks, explicit evidence requirements, and an accountable human reviewer.

Progress would mean: Review time and correction rates, together with the quality of the final evidence.

Who needs to be involved

Researchers, AI tool builders, domain reviewers, and program evaluators.

Research stage: Across the research journey.

More context

  • AI capability varies by task. Test it per task instead of trusting a model name.
  • Use deterministic checks where requirements are explicit. Use qualified human judgment where interpretation is needed.
  • Budget verification capacity alongside acceleration. One without the other produces volume, not knowledge.

Evidence and technical detail

Two working examples from this portfolio show the shape of the answer.

  1. Pre-set gates. The Mojo accuracy limits were frozen before the run. When Float32 failed, the failure stood. A later scientifically justified change requires a new protocol; the original failure remains on record.
  2. Retained corrections. An earlier finding of TOOLCHAIN_ABSENT was later corrected: an agent had checked global binaries and missed an existing Pixi environment. The record keeps both the wrong diagnosis and the correction, so the next person does not repeat it.

The capability-manifest idea belongs here too: if a model or agent declares what it can do in a structured, testable form, verification can be planned instead of improvised.

Sources: Retest report with correction

Connected research records

How can existing resources connect and scale without losing their custodians or context?

My example

A Unified Research Library could connect existing repositories through a shared catalog. Original custodians would keep their data, permissions, and expertise.

Make it easier to find a question, its evidence, and what was learned across projects.

proposed

A practical next step

Start with a small shared catalog that points to original records and preserves permissions, attribution, corrections, and disagreements.

Progress would mean: Time to find relevant evidence; usable cross-references; fewer missing source records.

Who needs to be involved

Repository custodians, librarians, researchers, and standards partners.

Research stage: Discovery → Reuse.

More context

  • Link protocols, attempts, code, environments, results, reviews, and later decisions.
  • Preserve custodianship, attribution, licensing, and access restrictions.
  • Record why an attempt stopped and what would be needed to continue.
  • Keep negative results that resolve uncertainty, alongside implementation and infrastructure failures.
  • Do not treat a missing record as proof that an experiment never ran. Use unknown.

Evidence and technical detail

Start with interoperable records, stable source identifiers, and a small shared vocabulary. Preserve licensing, attribution, access restrictions, corrections, and disagreements. AI could propose categories and related records; deterministic checks can enforce structure, while people review ambiguous interpretations.

Records reconstructed later must be labeled as reconstruction, not preregistration.

Sources: Registered Reports

Learning and continued support

When does continued support build capability, and when does it become dependency?

My example

An experiment may be blocked, completed with mixed results, or outside a tool’s valid range. One pass/fail label cannot explain all of that.

In the documented Mojo test, agreement passed; Float64 accuracy passed; Float32 accuracy failed. The overall protocol still failed.

documented

Sources: S02-I report

The Mojo result illustrates how to report a mixed technical outcome. It is not an SBIR award evaluation and does not establish a case for continued funding.

A practical next step

Record what another attempt changed: uncertainty resolved, capability gained, transition achieved, or a justified stop. Review this alongside commercial or mission progress.

Progress would mean: Evidence of learning and transition, with reasons for continuation, redirection, or stopping.

Who needs to be involved

Program evaluators, researchers, entrepreneurs, customers, and funding partners.

Research stage: Validation → Commercialization → Impact.

The SBIR discussion: hold both questions open

Cohen, Feldman, and Stern emphasize mission, capability, and stable support. Schönander asks how the wider ecosystem and opportunities for newcomers affect translation. Katz puts more weight on commercialization and graduation. The Murphy interview emphasizes results, learning, and transition.

Together, these perspectives invite a stronger review question: what did another award or attempt change? Documented learning can complement commercial or mission progress; it is not an automatic reason to keep funding the same work.

Evidence and technical detail

Foundations already exist. OSF supports research registration. Registered Reports evaluate research plans before results are known. The distinctive addition here is an interoperable record of execution, outcomes, reasons, and subsequent decisions, kept as separate dimensions rather than one pass/fail flag.

DimensionExample values
ExecutionPlanned, not started, blocked, running, completed, aborted
ValidityValid, invalid, uncertain, outside applicable domain
FindingSupports claim, contradicts claim, mixed, inconclusive, not evaluated
Criterion resultsBackend parity passed; accuracy failed; timing unevaluated
ReasonResource unavailable, toolchain problem, implementation defect, precision limit, insufficient data
ReviewUnreviewed, machine-checked, human-reviewed, disputed
Subsequent decisionContinue, revise protocol, replicate, pause, retire
Record historyCurrent, corrected, superseded, withdrawn

Each classification keeps its source passage or artifact, applicable rule version, reviewer, and date. Distinguish when the experiment happened from when its record was reconstructed or published. Retrospective reconstruction is never labeled preregistration.

The Mojo campaign is the worked example: backend parity passed, Float64 accuracy passed, Float32 accuracy failed, timing unevaluated, overall protocol failed, decision: continue with Float64 and study Float32 separately. One label would have lost all of that.

Sources: Center for Open Science, Registered Reports

Evidence stewardship

What infrastructure makes a result accessible and understandable later?

My example

Large research artifacts need affordable storage, findable metadata, integrity checks, and links that last. Capacity alone does not make evidence understandable or reproducible.

A practical next step

Connect reports to retained artifacts, integrity checks, clear access terms, and a named custodian.

Progress would mean: An authorized reviewer can find, verify, and interpret the retained record.

Who needs to be involved

Researchers, repositories, storage providers, and data stewards.

Research stage: Validation → Reuse.

More context

  • Independent researchers need clear guidance on eligibility, costs, retention, and preservation responsibilities.
  • Pair storage allocations with curation and preservation help.

Evidence and technical detail

The supplied Mojo explainer identifies an externally retained raw record that this presentation has not independently inspected. The general stewardship need is clear: connect a report to identifiable artifacts, integrity checks, retention terms, and a usable access path.

A storage allocation becomes more useful when another researcher can locate and understand the evidence, subject to its access and licensing rules.

Exploratory research

How can early exploratory work be understandable without overstating readiness?

My example

This is exploratory computational research with explicit limits. Its value for the Roadmap is the practice, not the hypothesis: numerical checks, failed attempts, corrections, and open questions are all kept and shown.

Exploratory work can produce useful methods and infrastructure even when its motivating hypothesis stays unproven.

documented

Mathematics and code only; no demonstration of physical feasibility.

Sources: Warp Field Notebook

A practical next step

Use a bounded notebook to separate the question, assumptions, mathematical or code results, and unresolved tests.

Progress would mean: A reviewer can distinguish an exploratory result from a validated application.

Who needs to be involved

Researchers, technical reviewers, and possible collaborators.

Research stage: Discovery → Translation.

More context

  • Present it as exploratory research with stated limitations.
  • Show how numerical checks, failed attempts, corrections, and unresolved questions are retained.
  • Highlight reusable tooling and validation methods produced along the way.
  • Add an experiment ledger with dates, protocol versions, criterion-level outcomes, reasons, and evidence links.
  • Distinguish contemporaneous records from later reconstruction.

Evidence and technical detail

Three exhibit records the logs already support:

  1. An experiment blocked by an incorrect environment diagnosis, later corrected.
  2. A port that matched its reference implementation but failed an independent accuracy requirement.
  3. Correct numerical output with unresolved or insufficient performance evidence.

For each ledger row: experiment and attempt IDs, execution date, protocol version, code and environment identifiers, criterion-level outcomes, reason codes, evidence links, and corrections. Where the logs do not establish whether something ran, the ledger says unknown.

Neither backend agreement nor the stencil qualification demonstrates a realizable propulsion system. That sentence stays attached to the notebook wherever it is presented.

Sources: Computational-Spacetime-Dynamics-Research · temporal-modulation-alcubierre

My example

The proposed convening exhibit would let a visitor inspect one research record: what was tested, what happened, which evidence supports it, and what changed after review.

The participant workflow is in development. This presentation is not a live Observatory connection.

in development

A practical next step

Test a reviewed, sanitized research record as a small exhibit before claiming a ready participant workflow.

Progress would mean: Visitors can explain the test, result, evidence, and remaining uncertainty.

Community partnerships

How can research institutions build useful, lasting relationships with communities?

My example

Florida Armored Combat is a nonprofit whose members include veterans, parents, blue-collar and white-collar workers, and people from many backgrounds. We have a community and worthwhile questions about belonging, recreation, participation barriers, and retention. We do not have a research partner.

Question for the room. Where does a nonprofit go when it has a community and good questions, but no research partner?

Community observations suggest questions; they do not establish health benefits or causation.

A practical next step

Use Florida Armored Combat as a possible partner for shaping a research question together, before choosing a method or making an outcome claim.

Progress would mean: A jointly defined question, clear roles, an agreed method, and a useful return to the community.

Who needs to be involved

Community members, researchers, and an accountable institutional partner.

Research stage: Discovery → Validation.

More context

  • Community observations can generate research questions. They do not by themselves establish effectiveness or causation.
  • Researchers and community members should develop the questions together.
  • Initial support should help establish partnerships, design studies, and arrange appropriate oversight.

Evidence and technical detail

A possible next step: ask a research institution for a community-engagement consultation. The University of Florida Clinical and Translational Science Institute provides a community engagement entry point to investigate. A sensible first project would ask why adults join, remain, or leave, and what benefits or barriers they perceive, including former participants so current members alone do not distort the picture. The institution determines review and consent requirements before any recruitment.

A short partnership brief would cover FAC's activities and locations, the membership diversity, questions members want answered, what FAC can contribute (relationships, facilities, organizational knowledge), and what it needs (study design, independent analysis, research oversight).

This is the portal use case in miniature. The request is not money first. It is a named person who can make the introduction and stay responsible for it.

Sources: UF CTSI community entry point · Florida Armored Combat

Agenda connection: Resource Guide, p. 14. Suggested breakout: Track B · Ecosystem best practices. Track placement and proposals are my contributions; the handouts provide the discussion context.

Technical assistance

What expertise is missing between a research result and a usable tool?

My example

Some projects need hands-on engineering help to become usable and maintainable: research software engineering, validation, deployment, security, data stewardship, documentation. Define that service and its users before deciding whether it needs a new institution.

Question for the room. Who helps promising work cross the distance between a working prototype and something others can rely on?

A practical next step

Pilot a small engineering and validation service with clear intake, scope, ownership, and handoff.

Progress would mean: Useful handoffs, reproducible work, external adoption, and a maintenance plan.

Who needs to be involved

Research software engineers, domain specialists, maintainers, and regional partners.

Research stage: Translation → Validation → Adoption.

More context

  • NSF already has a technology-and-translation directorate, TIP, whose role includes partnerships with industry, nonprofits, civil society, and communities of practice.
  • The proposed addition is accessible engineering assistance: research software engineering and maintenance, reproducibility and independent validation, secure deployment, data stewardship, help moving prototypes into sustained use.
  • Test it as a funded network of technical assistance centers coordinated through existing structures. A new federal institution is a much larger claim that has not been shown necessary.

Evidence and technical detail

How the three proposals fit together: the portal is the entry point, the technical network provides the assistance, and the research library preserves the evidence and learning. An Observatory exhibit could illustrate the research-record part of the proposal.

Evidence you can open

These six repositories are the starting points identified in the supplied materials. Specific result claims should be checked against their dated reports. Repository access and current readiness may vary.

  • Computational-Spacetime-Dynamics-Research: the research campaign records
  • KosMojAMD: the Mojo on AMD modernization case study
  • gkos-standard: the evidence-governance pre-standard
  • GKOS-Engine: the TypeScript reference engine
  • GKOS-Engine-Rust: the Rust implementation effort
  • GKOS-Observatory: the demonstration

What useful evidence records should preserve:

  • Exact experiment and source identifiers.
  • Failed, blocked, superseded, and inconclusive outcomes.
  • Original timestamps, with execution date kept separate from publication date.
  • Hardware, software, and environment boundaries.
  • Links from summaries to the underlying reports, manifests, logs, and artifacts.
  • Corrections as visible successor records, never silent rewrites.
  • Explicit separation of backend agreement, scientific accuracy, performance, and production readiness.

Related work, identified in the supplied materials, with current status requiring review: LLM_Engine_Rust-Over-GGML (archived comparison), LLM_Engine_Mojo, LLM_Engine_MojoRust (gated rebuild), GKOS-Engine-Lite, gkos-hindsight-governance, model-capability-manifest-standard, Kosmos-Oden, Kosmos-Oden-Lite, Kosmos_Research_Studio_Lite, Marshal-008-OS, theMarshal-Core-Rust, Hypatia, temporal-modulation-alcubierre, Paper01.

The three Rust/Mojo engine repositories overlap historically. Their roles and evidence boundaries need to be reconciled so a visitor can tell immediately what was attempted, what was measured, what was learned, and which repository now carries the authoritative evidence.

Before any private repository goes public it gets a disclosure review: credentials, personal data, internal network details, large artifacts, licensing, and any claim that exceeds the retained evidence.

Three pilot proposals

  • Point to an existing pathway. If a program already serves independent contributors well, say which one and how someone gets in.
  • Offer technical review. Pick one repository and check whether its claims match its evidence.
  • Connect a research partner. FAC has a community and questions. It needs a study-design collaborator.
  • Help shape a pilot. Portal, technical assistance network, or federated research records.

For the Roadmap facilitators, the asks map onto the seven breakout points and Tracks A through D. See the mid-level and deep views of each talking point for the track tags.
